cues.text: January thirtieth, seventeen oh three.
Edo, the future Tokyo.

In the middle of the night, forty-seven
armed men storm the home of a
high-ranking official.

They break through the guards and search
the rooms.
But the owner is nowhere to be found.
He is the only man they want.

And to kill him, they are willing to pay
with their own lives.

But here is the strange part: their enemy
did not kill the lord they are
avenging.

It was their lord who tried to kill him
first.

So why did forty-seven samurai decide to
finish someone else's fight?

And how did a killing that the state
condemned

as a crime become a symbol of loyalty for
three centuries?
It all began with two sword strikes.
April twenty-first, seventeen oh one.

At the shogun's castle, preparations are
underway for a reception for envoys
from the imperial court.

Among those taking part is the young lord
of Ako, Asano Naganori.

In a corridor, he approaches an official
named Kira Yoshinaka.

Kira is responsible for ceremonial
protocol.
He is talking to someone else.

Before he can even understand what is
happening, Asano draws a short sword.
The first strike wounds Kira.
He tries to escape.

Asano attacks again, but an official
standing nearby restrains him.
It is over in moments.
Kira is alive.
Asano is under arrest.
Why did he attack?

A witness heard Asano speak of a recent
grievance.

Later, stories would emerge about bribes
and humiliation.
But we do not know the true cause.

To the government, something else matters
more:

Asano drew a weapon in the ruler's castle
during a state ceremony,
and struck a man who had not attacked him.
The sentence comes that same day.
Asano must commit seppuku: ritual suicide.
His lands are confiscated.
Kira goes unpunished.

One failed strike has destroyed an entire
samurai house.

And the consequences fall on people who
were not even in that palace corridor.
They did not attack Kira.
They did not disobey orders.

Yet in a matter of hours, they lose the
position on
which their families' futures depend.

In Ako, hundreds of men suddenly lose
their lord, their service,
and their income.
They become ronin: masterless samurai.
What now?

Some propose defending the castle by
force.

Others consider following their lord into
death.

But the samurai Horibe Yasubei demands
something else: kill Kira.
Asano is dead.
His house has been destroyed.

Yet the man he fought is still living
freely.

To Horibe, leaving that fight unfinished
means accepting dishonor.

But Oishi Kuranosuke remains the leading
figure among the former retainers.

And he makes a decision that outrages
those demanding revenge.

Oishi surrenders the castle to the
authorities.
He refuses to attack Kira immediately.

For those who wanted a battle, this is a
bitter blow.

Their lord is dead, and his chief adviser
is voluntarily handing over the
family castle.

But armed resistance would mean defying
the shogunate itself,

and endangering people who can still be
saved.

He is not doing this because he has
nothing left to lose.

He is doing it because he still has
another way forward.
Asano has a younger brother, Daigaku.

If the shogunate allows him to lead a
restored Asano house,

the former retainers may be able to
preserve at least part of their old world.
Without another killing.

The ronin now have two leaders, and two
answers to the same question.

Horibe believes honor can only be restored
with blood.

Oishi is looking for a way to save the
family.
Their dispute becomes a race against time.

While Oishi seeks a decision on Daigaku,
those in favor of an attack discuss
how to reach Kira.
But the official's home is well defended.

A rushed assault could leave the attackers
dead while Kira survives.
Months pass.
The former retainers scatter.
Some look for a new lord to serve.

The longer the wait, the fewer men are
willing to gamble with their future.
At last, an answer comes.
July, seventeen oh two.
Daigaku is released from house arrest.

But the domain of Ako is not returned to
him.

He is placed under the supervision of
relatives.

The attempt to restore the house has
failed.

We will never know whether Oishi believed
that attempt would succeed.

But now he and his supporters begin
preparing an attack on Kira.

That does not mean they have no other
choice.

The ronin could go their separate ways,
find new service, and start again.

But for some, that would mean abandoning
everything they understand as duty.
And now Oishi is among them.

Making the decision is easier than finding
men willing to carry it out.

They understand that even if they kill
Kira, the authorities may execute them.
Their families could be punished too.

One of the future attackers, Otaka Gengo,
writes a farewell letter to his
mother.
He warns her of the danger.

He also admits that Asano had never shown
him any special personal favor.

He is not walking toward death because his
lord once saved his life.

His motives are more complicated: duty,
honor,
and obligations to his comrades.

Not every former retainer is willing to
pay that price.
Some refuse.
In the end, forty-seven men remain.

Among them is Horibe, who has demanded
revenge from the start.
Oishi himself.
And his young son, Chikara.

Now Oishi is risking more than his own
life.

He once tried to preserve the Asano house
so that his men would not die in a
pointless fight.

Now he is leading them into an attack from
which they may never return.

That does not make his first decision a
lie.

But it shows how much the situation has
changed.

Before they attack, they must discover
where Kira is, choose the right moment,
and get past his guards.

The official himself knows that someone
may seek revenge.

If he slips away, all their preparations
will have been for nothing.

At last, the night of January thirtieth,
seventeen oh three arrives.
The ronin attack Kira's residence.
Fighting breaks out inside.

The defenders resist, but the attackers
advance through the house.

Then comes the worst discovery: Kira is
nowhere to be found.

They have risked their lives to reach one
man.

But if he escapes, all they will have left
is a charge of armed assault.
The ronin search again and again.

They go through the rooms and check hiding
places.
Defeating the guards is not enough.

They must be certain that this is the very
man they came to find.

With every moment spent searching, there
is a chance that Kira has already

escaped while the fighting continued
inside.
At last, they find the owner of the house.

Twenty-two months earlier, Asano tried to
kill him in the palace.
Kira survived.
This time, there is no escape.
They kill Kira and cut off his head.
Their revenge is complete.
But the victors do not flee Edo.

Instead, they carry Kira's head through
the city to Sengakuji Temple,
to Asano's grave.

There, they place it before their dead
lord.
They have done what Asano could not.
And now they are ready to answer for it.

But of the forty-seven participants, only
forty-six surrender to the
authorities.
One ronin, Terasaka, has left the others.
We do not know for certain why.
He will outlive his comrades by decades.

The others must wait for a decision the
authorities are in no hurry to make.
Until now, they have acted as one unit.

They knew their target, prepared the
attack, and carried it out.

Now they have neither a plan nor a weapon
that can change the outcome.

All they can do is wait for the state to
judge their actions.

On one hand, forty-six men have killed an
official whom the state had not
found guilty.

Acquit them, and any band of samurai could
overturn the government's decisions
by the sword.

On the other hand, the ronin did not try
to seize power or Kira's property.

They did not run once they had achieved
their goal.

To many of their contemporaries, their
actions looked like extraordinary
devotion.

Can you admire their loyalty and still
consider them killers?
A week passes.
Then another.

The ronin remain in custody, not knowing
whether they will live.

On March twentieth, seventeen oh three,
the shogunate announces its decision:
all forty-six must commit seppuku.

It is a death sentence, though they are
allowed to die in a manner befitting
their samurai rank.

That same day, Horibe, Oishi, and his son
Chikara die.

Along with the others, they are buried
beside Asano.

Horibe has achieved the revenge he
demanded from the start.

Oishi tried to save the house without more
bloodshed,

and ended up leading even his own son to
his death.

But this is where the story begins its
second life.

Over the years, the ronin become the
heroes of plays, books,
and eventually films.

In seventeen forty-eight comes the famous
play, Kanadehon Chushingura.

The image of loyal retainers gradually
overshadows the uncomfortable facts of
the real case.

Revenge makes a compelling story: a long
wait, a dangerous attack,
a willingness to sacrifice everything.

And the easier the story becomes to tell,
the easier it is to forget the
question that started it all.

In the legend, it is simple: noble
warriors avenged their lord
and sacrificed their lives.
The reality is more complicated.
We do not know why Asano attacked Kira.

We do not know whether Kira had wronged
him.

And the surviving letters do not allow us
to assume that all the ronin shared
the same motive.
But we do know what they did.

Forty-seven men decided to finish a fight
their lord had started.
Forty-six paid for it with their lives.
The state called their actions a crime.

Generations remembered them as a model of
loyalty.

And the story's central question remains
unanswered:

if someone is willing to die for his
honor,

does that mean he has the right to kill
someone else for it?
